section_summary: This section comprises political and economic reporting from the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State covering February, March, and April 1940. It includes the concluding portions of the February monthly report and its associated schedules of outgoing communications, an internal Far Eastern Affairs memorandum, the full March monthly report (Despatch No. 4681), and the opening portion of the April monthly report (Despatch No. 4715). The documents reflect mounting Japanese-American friction over the inauguration of the Wang Ching-wei regime in Nanking, Japanese military strikes on American mission properties and the Haiphong-Yunnan Railway, the status quo of the Netherlands East Indies, and Japan's internal legislative and economic mobilization.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on economic and political conditions in Japan for February 1940, accompanied by schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington.
subfiles.summary: This document contains the concluding sections of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for February 1940, detailing fertilizer supply regulations, fiber goods distribution control, commodity price increases, and foreign trade balances. It outlines labor diversion ordinances under the National General Mobilization Law, the planned dissolution of trade unions, and Diet debates over declining labor productivity. Comprehensive schedules list all despatches (Nos. 4459-4549) and telegrams (Nos. 69-148) sent during February, documenting developments such as the Asama Maru affair, the bombing of the Yunnan Railway, the detention of journalist James R. Young, and the parliamentary controversy surrounding Takao Saito.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 4611: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of February 1940 (Report No. 161)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum noting key sections of Tokyo Despatch No. 4681 regarding March 1940 conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Prepared by Ivan B. White of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, this memorandum directs departmental attention to specific topics in Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 4681. It highlights Embassy analysis on Japanese sentiments regarding potential U.S. involvement in the European war, Japanese trade negotiations with the Netherlands East Indies, and the approved Japanese national budget for 1940-1941.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 4681

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 162 on political, international, military, and economic conditions in Japan during March 1940, with schedules of communications sent.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the Embassy's comprehensive review of conditions in Japan for March 1940, focusing on growing tensions with the United States over China and the non-treaty commercial situation. The report examines Japanese attacks on the Haiphong-Yunnan Railway, the inauguration of Wang Ching-wei's regime at Nanking and the U.S. non-recognition statement, Anglo-Japanese negotiations over Tientsin silver, and the dispatch of economic missions to Italy and Latin America. Domestically, it chronicles the expulsion of Takao Saito from the Diet, Major General Akira Muto's warnings on political parties and totalitarianism, enactment of the record 10.5 billion yen budget, expanded commodity price controls, and lists of despatches and telegrams forwarded during the month.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 4681: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of March 1940 (Report No. 162)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 163 reviewing internal and international conditions in Japan during April 1940.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Report No. 163 detailing Japanese internal affairs and foreign relations during April 1940. The report surveys sharp Japanese official and press reactions to Secretary of State Cordell Hull's statement rejecting the Wang Ching-wei regime at Nanking, diplomatic pronouncements concerning the status quo of the Netherlands East Indies, and Japanese protests over Philippine immigration restrictions. It records formal American representations against renewed aerial bombings of American missions in China and blockade indignities at Tientsin, while noting Japanese sensitivity and defiant press commentary regarding U.S. Pacific Fleet maneuvers and congressional testimony by Admirals Stark and Taussig.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 4715: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of April 1940 (Report No. 163)
